scenes.text: So, what makes a fitness test worth running? A squad does the beep test in week one and again in week ten, and every score has gone up. The coach says the training program worked. Write down two other reasons the scores might have risen. Then write one thing you'd need to control to rule them out.

In Year 11 you met two checks on any measurement: validity, whether it measures what it claims to, and reliability, whether it gives the same result again when the athlete hasn't changed. Testing adds two more. Specificity: does the test match this sport's demands? Timing a rower over a forty-metre sprint fails that. Objectivity: would two testers score it the same? A coach judging technique by eye fails that. A vertical jump is a valid test of leg power, and an invalid test of endurance, however carefully you run it. Reliability is bought with protocol, the fixed conditions, equipment and scoring rules. Same surface, shoes, time of day, warm-up and scorer. Each one you hold constant removes a rival explanation. That's why an unreliable test is worse than no test. It produces a number that looks like evidence.

Testing starts from a question, not a test. Which quality is limiting this athlete right now? Name it, and the test follows. Aerobic capacity, a shuttle run. Strength, a one-rep max, the heaviest load lifted once. Power, a vertical jump. Speed, a timed sprint.

The syllabus names two tests for a reason. The Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test isn't a continuous run. Shuttles alternate with short active rests, so it measures what team-sport players need: repeated efforts with incomplete recovery. The Wingate test is a thirty-second, all-out anaerobic sprint on a bike against a fixed resistance. It reports peak power, mean power, and how far power drops by the end. Say a cyclist peaks at a thousand watts and finishes at six hundred. The drop is four hundred, divided by a thousand, so a forty per cent fatigue index.

The syllabus names two groups, and they want different things from testing. For a recreational participant, testing is about health, motivation and a safe starting point. The measures are simple: resting heart rate, blood pressure, waist size, and a submaximal aerobic estimate, where the person never works flat out. It only needs to catch a meaningful health change, every few months. For an elite athlete, testing diagnoses performance and informs selection. The measures are sport-specific, precise enough that the test's own error is smaller than the small changes that matter at the top level, and repeated through the season. And the risks differ. A maximal test can put a beginner off exercise, while for an elite athlete the cost is lost training time. So recreational testing supports health and participation, and elite testing earns its place only if it changes a decision.

Now, how assessment builds the program. It does four separate jobs. First, it sets the baseline, the first measurement that every later one is compared with. Intensity is set as a share of something measured, like the maximum heart rate from Year 11, or a one-rep max. Without a baseline, it's a guess. Second, it finds the limiter, the component holding performance back. Third, it makes the goal specific, a target score on a test the athlete has already done. Fourth, it closes the loop. Re-testing with the same protocol is the only evidence the block worked. A seventeen-year-old club netballer has a strong Yo-Yo score, an average vertical jump, and a big difference between legs on a single-leg hop. So the block puts lower-body power first, adds single-leg work, keeps aerobic work at maintenance, and re-tests both jumps, on the same surface, in the same shoes.

A result has four limits. Motivation is part of the score: trying harder the second time raises it with no change in fitness. Protocol drifts. Surface, shoes, heat, time of day, and who's counting all move a score. Ecological validity, how well a test copies the real sport, is limited. A bike in a lab has no tackles, decisions or changes of direction. And a test measures a component, not an athlete. Now back to the coach's beep test. Four rival explanations compete with the training. The fix isn't to stop testing. Standardise the protocol, judge change against normal variation, and read the results beside what the coach sees in games.
Two things to remember. Name the limiter, then pick the test. And every program answer runs baseline, limiter, target, re-test.

Two exam questions. First. A fifty-eight-year-old is starting supervised exercise after years of inactivity, cleared at Stage 1 screening. A fifteen-year-old swimmer wants to know whether her eight-week aerobic block worked. For each, choose a test, name the component, and justify it. Pause here to answer.

For the fifty-eight-year-old, a submaximal aerobic test with simple strength and flexibility checks, because a maximal test isn't needed and could put them off. For the swimmer, repeat a timed four-hundred-metre swim with her baseline's exact protocol, because the decision is about change. The classic mistake is giving the beginner a maximal beep test.

Second. A sixteen-year-old rugby league halfback's pre-season percentiles: Yo-Yo, eighty-fifth. Sprint, fortieth. Vertical jump, thirty-fifth. Predicted squat maximum, thirtieth. Sit-and-reach, seventieth. Identify the limiter, what to only maintain, and two tests to repeat, each with one condition held constant. Pause here to answer.

The limiter is lower-body strength and power, the two lowest ranks, and they agree with each other. Aerobic fitness, at the eighty-fifth, is kept at maintenance, a deliberate choice that gives time to the limiter. Re-test the jump and the squat, same surface and shoes for the jump, same depth rule for the squat. The classic mistake is training everything equally.

So choose the test from the limiter, run it the same way every time, and let the result set the baseline, the target and the re-test. Now say the cycle finds this for a track cyclist: anaerobic power is the limiter. How do anaerobic training methods differ?
